summary: Gives an overview of Source-Specific Multicast and issues around deploying it. It covers how this service model eases the challenges of inter-domain multicast, what changes routing protocols and applications need, and interoperability issues. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) lets a receiver request multicast traffic from a named source to a named group. This can simplify multicast routing because the network builds a tree from that source and does not need the shared-tree machinery used by Any-Source Multicast.

subtitle: An overview of multicast channels identified by both a source and a group address.

tldr.problem: In Any-Source Multicast, receivers identify a group but not its senders, creating challenges for address allocation, access control, and inter-domain routing.
tldr.mechanism: Source-Specific Multicast identifies a channel by a source address S and group address G. Receivers request that pair, and routers build source-rooted forwarding trees.
tldr.outcome: SSM removes the need for a shared-tree rendezvous point and MSDP for SSM service. RFC 3569 is an overview of SSM and deployment issues, not its standard specification.

today: RFC 3569 is an Informational RFC published in July 2003. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the document says it is an overview rather than the SSM standard.

sections.title: A Multicast Channel Names Its Source
sections.content:
In Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), a channel is identified by a source address S and a destination group address G. A source sends datagrams to G, and a receiver subscribes to the pair (S,G). The channel has one source and can have any number of receivers.

The RFC identifies 232/8 for IPv4 SSM and FF3x::/96 for IPv6 SSM. It describes subscriptions using IGMP version 3 for IPv4 and MLD version 2 for IPv6. This document provides an overview and deployment discussion, not the SSM standard.
sections.plainLanguage: An SSM receiver names both the group it wants and the source it wants to hear from. This gives the network enough information to deliver that source's multicast traffic.

sections.title: How Any-Source Multicast Works
sections.content:
In Any-Source Multicast (ASM), a group is identified by a destination address. Any host can send to the group, and a receiver joining it can receive data from any source.

The RFC describes a commonly used ASM suite involving IGMP, PIM Sparse Mode, MSDP, and MBGP. PIM-SM can use a shared tree rooted at a rendezvous point (RP); MSDP lets RPs in different domains announce sources. These mechanisms support a model in which receivers do not have to name a source when joining.
sections.plainLanguage: With ASM, a receiver joins a group without naming a sender. The routing system may use a shared tree and rendezvous points to connect senders and receivers.

sections.title: Problems SSM Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC identifies address allocation as a problem for ASM: different applications can choose the same group address. SSM distinguishes (S1,G) from (S2,G), so a channel is tied to its source as well as its group.

SSM also lets a receiver request traffic from only a named source. This makes it harder for another source to send unwanted traffic to that channel, although source-address spoofing remains possible. Because the source is known, SSM needs source-based forwarding trees rather than shared trees; the RFC says it does not require the RP-based shared-tree infrastructure or MSDP.
sections.plainLanguage: Including the source in the channel name separates channels that use the same group address. It also lets receivers choose a sender and lets routers build a path directly from that sender.

sections.title: Applications and Host Reporting
sections.content:
An SSM application must know both S and G before it subscribes. Finding those addresses is the application's responsibility; the RFC gives web pages and session-announcement applications as possible ways to provide them, and leaves the discovery method outside its scope.

The host must be able to pass the source and destination addresses to its network layer. IGMPv3 and MLDv2 provide source-filtering reports needed to request a channel; earlier versions described in the RFC allow a host to name only the group.
sections.plainLanguage: An application needs to learn both addresses before it can request a channel. The host then reports the chosen source and group to the network using a source-filtering protocol.

sections.title: Router Rules for SSM
sections.content:
For a group address in the SSM range, a designated router that receives an (S,G) join MUST send an (S,G) join, never a shared-tree (*,G) join. Backbone routers MUST NOT propagate (*,G) joins for groups in that range.

Rendezvous points MUST NOT accept PIM Register messages or (*,G) Join messages for SSM-range groups. These rules prevent ASM shared-tree behavior from being applied to SSM addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: For an SSM channel, routers follow the named source rather than joining a shared tree. The RFC lists rules that keep rendezvous points and backbone routers from using ASM behavior for SSM addresses.

sections.title: Coexistence and Security
sections.content:
SSM is the service model for the SSM address range; ASM can continue on other addresses. An (S,G) join outside that range is allowed, but the RFC says SSM service is not guaranteed there. MSDP remains relevant to ASM, and the RFC says RPs must not accept, originate, or forward MSDP Source-Active messages for SSM-range groups.

The RFC says SSM adds no new security considerations for IP multicast. It can help prevent denial-of-service traffic from unwanted sources, but it does not guarantee protection against such attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: SSM and ASM can operate in different address ranges. SSM makes unwanted sources harder to use, but it does not guarantee protection against attacks.
